Soil and fecal samples were collected periodically for 120 days after grazing. Enrichment, selective culture and PCR were used for STEC and Salmonella enterica detection. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was assessed using microdilution assays, and whole genome sequencing (WGS) was used to characterize AMR genes, virulence genes and population structure. All 284 soil and 79 fecal samples collected tested negative for Salmonella enterica and E. coli O157. Presumptive STEC was detected by colony PCR in 3.2% (n = 9/284, 95% CI 1.7-5.9%) of the soil samples, and 34.2% (n = 27/79, 95% CI 24.7-45.2%) of fecal samples. Shiga toxin genes were confirmed by WGS in 15 of 31 sequenced isolates. Predominant subtypes were stx1c and stx2b, and O176:H4 and O174:H2 were the most common serotypes. Phenotypic AMR was detected in 33.3% (n = 12/36) of isolates, with multidrug resistance in 8.3% (n = 3/36). A soil and a sheep fecal isolate differed by one core-genome single nucleotide polymorphism and shared a closed multidrug-resistance plasmid of identical gene content, consistent with a lineage resident in the flock that transferred to soil. Confirmed STEC in orchard soil was rare and transient. These results provide evidence to inform food safety guidelines on crops integrated with livestock.

papers.title: SIRT3 preserves mitochondrial DNA integrity to restrain cGAS-STING signaling and autoimmune inflammation
papers.abstract: Mitochondria play critical roles beyond energy production, including regulation of innate immunity through release of damage-associated molecular patterns such as mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3), a mitochondrial deacetylase, modulates mitochondrial function, reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, and inflammation. Here, we investigate the role of SIRT3 in controlling Type I interferon (IFN) responses in macrophages. We show that Sirt3 depletion in mouse macrophages increases basal mtDNA release into the cytosol, activating the cGAS-STING pathway and enhancing the expression of IFN-{beta} and downstream interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). Accordingly, Sirt3-deficient cells exhibit markedly increased resistance to vesicular stomatitis virus infection. Secreted IFN-{beta} also acts in a paracrine manner, priming neighboring cells and reinforcing antiviral defenses. Using mtDNA-deficient ({rho}0) cells, we demonstrate that intact mtDNA is essential for this amplified interferon response, as mtDNA depletion abolishes IFN-{beta} induction following Sirt3 knockdown. Mechanistically, increased mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) in SIRT3-deficient cells promotes mtDNA leakage and cGAS-STING activation, effects that are attenuated by the mitochondrial superoxide scavenger MitoTEMPO. In vivo, SIRT3 protects against chlorhexidine gluconate-induced peritoneal fibrosis by restraining macrophage infiltration, ISGs expression and fibrotic remodeling, underscoring its role in modulating STING-dependent inflammation and tissue damage. Finally, reanalysis of transcriptomic datasets from patients with lupus nephritis and rheumatoid arthritis reveals reduced SIRT3 expression, suggesting that SIRT3 downregulation is also associated with human inflammatory diseases. Collectively, our findings identify SIRT3 as an important regulator of mitochondrial integrity and oxidative stress that modulates innate immune and antiviral responses.

papers.title: Large language models recover archival pathology data and identify NSE as a candidate prognostic marker in Ewing sarcoma
papers.abstract: Background: Current risk stratification for Ewing sarcoma relies heavily on clinical factors such as metastatic status, failing to capture histologic heterogeneity as a potential prognostic indicator. Although pathology reports contain rich biological data, this information remains locked in unstructured narrative text, limiting large-scale retrospective analyses. We aimed to validate the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs) for scalable data abstraction and to identify prognostic histologic features from a large multi-institutional cohort. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using data from six Children's Oncology Group (COG) clinical trials. We utilized an LLM-based pipeline (OpenAI o3) to extract structured variables, including immunohistochemical (IHC) markers and CD99 staining patterns - from digitized, Optical Character Recognition (OCR)-processed pathology reports. Extraction accuracy was validated against a human-annotated ground truth (n=200) and cross-validated against senior experts (n=48). We assessed the association between extracted features and Overall Survival (OS) using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression, adjusting for metastatic status. Findings: We analyzed 931 diagnostic pathology reports spanning over 19-years. The LLM achieved a weighted average accuracy of 94% across 17 IHC markers; in a cross-validation subset, the LLM outperformed human annotators (weighted average accuracy over 15 IHC markers: LLM o3: 98.1%, a resident specialist 91.4%, and a senior expert 95.9%). Survival analysis identified Neuron-Specific Enolase (NSE) and S100 as significant prognostic biomarkers. After adjusting for metastatic status, NSE positivity was associated with significantly inferior survival (HR 2.15, 95% CI 1.15 - 4.02, p=0.016); this risk was most pronounced in patients with non-metastatic disease (HR 5.64, p=0.0055). Conversely, S100 positivity was associated with improved survival (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.34-1.00, p=0.046). Interpretation: LLM-assisted extraction of pathology variables is highly accurate and scalable, capable of unlocking "dark data" from historical clinical trials. We identified NSE as a potent risk factor and S100 as a protective marker in Ewing sarcoma, particularly in localized disease. These findings suggest that AI-derived histologic data can refine risk stratification and, if validated, warrant inclusion in future prospective trials.

papers.title: Linking in situ activity to fitness reveals that clinically-relevant factors underpin pathogen survival in environmental reservoirs
papers.abstract: Natural environments are a key reservoir for many opportunistic pathogens, yet mechanisms enabling survival within complex microbial communities remain poorly defined. Current approaches do not adequately link molecular understanding of bacterial survival to the activities of bacteria within natural microbial communities. Here we combine in situ community profiling with isolate-level functional genomics studies to understand how opportunistic pathogens from the genera Escherichia, Klebsiella and Enterococcus survive in urban-adjacent freshwater ecosystems. Potential pathogens from these genera were identified and isolated from urban freshwater, and targeted metatranscriptomics showed expression of genes involved in housekeeping, resistance and virulence functions in situ. We further investigated an E. coli isolate of ST73, a clinically-important lineage associated with urinary tract infections, showing that it is pathogenic in mice, and survives in freshwater microcosms for at least one month. Functional genomics investigations in freshwater containing autochthonous microbiota revealed genes involved in amino acid metabolism, nucleotide biosynthesis, and biogenesis of the virulence- and biofilm-associated surface amyloid curli as important survival determinants; many of these genes were also highly expressed in situ. Deletion of curli structural genes resulted in reduced pelagic biofilm formation and a fitness defect specifically in the presence of freshwater microbiota, which was reversed by carbon supplementation, indicating that curli promote E. coli freshwater through aggregation-mediated nutritional competition. This study deepens our understanding of pathogen survival in waterways, highlights the importance of natural environments for selection of clinically-important traits, and provides a broadly applicable framework for interrogating mechanisms of pathogen survival in complex environments and communities.

papers.title: Lacuna: Cryptic Binding Pocket Discovery via Conformational Ensemble Analysis
papers.abstract: Lacuna, an open-source Python tool for discovering cryptic binding pockets: sites that are absent or too small to detect in the unbound structure of a protein, RNA or DNA and open only during conformational fluctuation. Most binding-site predictors score a single static structure, the very structure in which a cryptic site is invisible. Lacuna generates a conformational ensemble from any input structure, detects pockets independently in every conformer, clusters the detections into persistent sites, and ranks those sites with a model fitted on within-structure pairs. Ensemble generation is pluggable: normal mode analysis (NMA) by default, with implicit-solvent molecular dynamics, Boltz-2 diffusion sampling or a user-supplied ensemble as alternatives. On the designated test fold of CryptoBench, all 222 structures of which are scored, the zero-dependency default recovers the cryptic site for 59.9% of structures in its top five predictions, and it recovers 69% on the PocketMiner set, 41% on a curated set of literature apo/holo pairs and 89% of structures in the already-open COACH420 set. On that test fold, ordering the candidate set with the fitted ranker rather than the analytic rule it replaced accounts for a gain of 27.5 points (95% CI +21.2 to +33.8), the largest single effect measured here. An optional protein-language-model (PLM) ranker reaches 66.1% on a 180-structure subset of that fold, and pooling the geometric detector with an optional learned surface detector raises top-five recovery to 73.9% and the fraction of structures in which the site is found at all to 86.4% in a separate held-out evaluation at five conformers (184 structures; both optional configurations measured with version 1.4.0). A new per-residue cryptic-site propensity reaches AUROC 0.766 and AUPRC 0.340 on the same test fold (231 targets), against 0.249 for the same scorer on the input structure alone, so the ensemble carries information the input does not. RNA and DNA need no extra flags; on RNA sites with no cavity in the input the ensemble raises the fraction found from 44% to 73% (measured with version 1.3.0). With the default NMA backend the pocket report is identical at any thread count and between Windows and Linux on the 40 proteins compared, ensemble generation needs less than half the memory of version 1.4.0 from 1,300 residues up, and the full pipeline is 7% to 30% faster than 1.4.0 on the reference proteins of the repository's speed table. At the default 20 conformers it takes a median of 1.9 seconds per chain on one CPU thread (30 chains of 57 to 676 residues). Outputs include docking-ready Boltz constraints and AutoDock Vina boxes, a per-residue propensity map and the conformer ensemble. Lacuna is MIT licensed, available at https://github.com/mooreneural/lacuna and on PyPI as lacuna-pockets, and runs as a local MCP server for AI assistants and on hosted no-install platforms.

papers.title: EcoXAI: Autonomous Agentic Ecosystem for Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Biomedical Discovery
papers.abstract: Motivation: As biomedical datasets and knowledge graphs continue to grow in size, complexity, and heterogeneity, navigating and extracting actionable insights from them presents a major bottleneck for researchers. There is a clear need for autonomous analytical solutions that can utilize recent advancements in agentic AI such as agent harnessing and loop engineering without introducing hallucination or workflow fragmentation. Researchers, regardless of technical expertise, need tools that streamline complex data analysis and deliver meaningful, actionable insights grounded in both data and established biomedical knowledge. EcoXAI addresses this by introducing a modular, customizable, containerized multi-agent system that structures analysis into explicit pipeline execution stages, lowering the computational barrier for clinical and translational researchers. Result: EcoXAI replaces monolithic AI text interfaces with an autonomous execution-driven framework with specialized bioinformatics agents for delivering proactive, data-driven insights grounded in established biological knowledge. Unlike purely LLM-driven or less integrated AI solutions prone to hallucinations or biologically implausible outcomes, EcoXAI's multi-agent framework, which leverages modern agentic management and explicit knowledge graph integration, provides greater transparency and verifiability in its reasoning. In our use case in drug repurposing for Alzheimer's Disease, EcoXAI evaluated 103 drug candidates and identified 79 novel candidates whose predictive models exceeded a randomized baseline, including the CCR5 antagonist Maraviroc, whose generated hypothesis was subsequently supported by the literature. These results demonstrate the potential of knowledge graph-grounded AI agents to accelerate hypothesis-driven biomedical research.

papers.title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence representations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacterial pathogens complicates infectious disease management. Protein sequences encode molecular features underlying resistance functions such as antibiotic inactivation and drug efflux, providing a basis for investigating bacterial AMR. Protein language models can extract transferable representations from these sequences. However, general purpose protein language models have limited capacity to represent AMR-associated sequences, while task-specific tools often address individual prediction problems. These limitations highlight the need for protein representations that better capture resistance associated functions and can be reused across complementary tasks, supporting systematic AMR analysis from sequence variation to functional relationships among proteins. We developed BacLLM, a language-guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder, enabling sequence only inference after training. Compared with baseline models, BacLLM provided more informative representations of resistance associated sequences, achieving a mean F1 score of 0.956 across six AMR benchmarks with logistic regression, 2.7 percentage points above the strongest baseline. It also captured resistance associated mutational signals at single residue resolution and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending the same representation framework to an intervention oriented application, BacLLM also improved strain level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a reusable protein representation framework for analyzing resistance associated sequence variation and functional organization, with applications in AMR surveillance and phage candidate prioritization.

papers.title: Wastewater metagenomic sequencing quantitatively tracks transmission dynamics for human pathogenic viruses
papers.abstract: Wastewater metagenomic sequencing theoretically characterizes all nucleic acids in a sample, but whether sequencing reads reflect transmission dynamics of circulating viruses in the contributing community is unknown. We evaluated if wastewater metagenomic sequencing data can be used to reconstruct transmission dynamics of endemic, routinely circulating viruses. Using deep, untargeted wastewater metagenomic sequencing data from four locations in the United States, we generated quantitative estimates of transmission dynamics (time-varying growth rate and effective reproduction number) within a Bayesian framework for widely monitored viruses. Across locations and viruses, estimates were statistically concordant with those derived from clinical surveillance and polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based wastewater monitoring data. Furthermore, we estimated growth rate from wastewater metagenomic sequencing data for numerous viruses not otherwise widely monitored, demonstrating the data expands the targets that can feasibly be monitored in parallel. Wastewater metagenomic sequencing can support both novel pathogen detection and routine surveillance of endemic pathogens.

papers.title: Integrated Genomic and Transcriptomic Profiling Reveals Distinct Biological Programs and Therapeutic Opportunities in Cancer of Unknown Primary
papers.abstract: Background: Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment. Methods: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Results: High-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity. WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features. WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients. Conclusions: CUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes. Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.

papers.title: Human-Agentic AI Collaboration Workflow for Trend Analysis of ChatGPT Applications in Healthcare
papers.abstract: Background: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated strong potential to transform healthcare research and practice. However, LLMs are probabilistic and generate inherently variable outputs, which create risk and uncertainty in healthcare applications. Therefore, analyzing the current research landscape of ChatGPT applications is imperative to understand applied techniques and related concerns and to facilitate their practical integration into healthcare information systems. Objective: Leveraging LLM-based agentic AI with domain experts to analyze trends in ChatGPT healthcare applications and to examine the collaborative and interpretative capacities of LLM agents in broader contexts beyond narrowly defined topics. Methods: The review used a systematic search of the PubMed and Web of Science databases, following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and focused on ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors. To support the review process, an adaptive, iterative LLM-based agentic AI with a human-in-the-loop mechanism was employed for automated metadata extraction, identification, classification, and knowledge synthesis. The extracted information was subsequently used for temporal and thematic analyses, citation network construction, and main-path analysis. Results: Across 192 papers, the review identified 511 ChatGPT application types, 690 concern items, and 368 influence usage factors distinct from traditional IT, achieving a metadata error rate of 1.04%. The human-agentic AI workflow enabled efficient synthesis of contextual information across studies, addressing the growing challenge of timely evidence integration in medical knowledge. The findings provide insights into the evolving trajectories of ChatGPT applications in healthcare and demonstrate the value of an expert-validated human-agentic AI workflow in supporting literature analysis and streamlining review processes. Conclusion: This review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors in healthcare. The study further provides meaningful insights into the operational mechanisms of agentic AI, demonstrating the potential of human-AI collaboration for medical informatics research.

papers.title: Evaluation of System One Models on Biomedical Texts
papers.abstract: Objective To compare the performance and cost of System One models (SOMs) with general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on biomedical tasks and evaluate confidence-based routing. Materials and Methods We evaluated three SOMs and three LLMs across seven datasets and eight endpoints covering question answering, error detection, structured extraction, and clinical-note assessment. Outcomes included task-specific performance, recorded inference cost and latency, and confidence calibration. Calibration data determined routing schemes and confidence thresholds to evaluate test predictions, with cost-matched random referral as a comparator. Results Claude Opus 5.5 had the highest primary performance on all eight endpoints. The strongest SOM, Jev, had competitive performance with the evaluated LLMs and cost less than 1% of Opus on most datasets. Three selected SOM-to-LLM routes reduced costs by 30.0%-71.7% relative to the receiving LLM, with modest reductions in performance. On one benchmark, SOM-to-SOM routing achieved 91.1% accuracy, compared with 82.3% and 82.2% for the individual models. Discussion SOMs offered favorable performance-cost tradeoffs for most tasks. The magnitude of the advantages depended on task structure and prompting requirements. Confidence-based routing between SOMs and LLMs can leverage complementary model strengths and offers additional flexibility in performance-cost tradeoffs. The price advantages offered by SOMs can facilitate experimentation and development of workflows. This warrants further evaluation on closed datasets. Conclusion For biomedical tasks with predefined choices, SOMs represent a competitive stand-alone or first-stage approach.

papers.title: Multi-Model Comparison of Deep and Classical Architectures for ECG Diagnostic Superclass Classification on PTB-XL
papers.abstract: Objective. It remains unclear which architecture best sorts 12-lead electrocardiograms into diagnostic superclasses, and whether added model complexity pays off. Methods. Using 21,375 PTB-XL records under one patient-level split, we compared a Mamba-style state space model, a residual convolutional network, a bidirectional long short-term memory network, a convolutional-recurrent network with attention, soft-voting ensembles of these networks, and MiniRocket features with LightGBM. Each record took the superclass of its highest-likelihood diagnostic code, and we scored saved predictions with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals. Results. No model clearly outperformed MiniRocket with LightGBM, which needs no graphics processor. The ensemble of the three deep models with the highest validation macro F1 score reached 0.656, against 0.645 for MiniRocket with LightGBM (difference +0.011, 95% confidence interval -0.007 to +0.031), and an ensemble of all four deep models reached 0.657. An exploratory ensemble, whose members we chose after seeing test results, reached 0.665 and was the only ensemble whose interval excluded zero (+0.021, 0.002 to 0.040); we regard that margin as optimistic. Hypertrophy was the hardest class (F1 0.33 to 0.41), and differences in its recall mostly reflected threshold placement. Conclusions. Under one shared split, deep ensembles added little over a classical pipeline. Significance. These results give biomedical informatics researchers a statistically grounded reference for judging whether complex models justify their cost on this benchmark. With one dataset, one split, one training seed per model, and no external validation, they do not show readiness for clinical use.

papers.title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children
papers.abstract: Background Misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. Methods Retrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by an LLM agent, Dr CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). Findings The median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, the LLM agent and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints. Interpretation Dr CaBot and attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians showed similar performance in generating differential diagnoses from clinical documentation, suggesting potential as a diagnostic aid. Whether this performance improves care, particularly outside pediatric specialty centers, requires prospective evaluation.

papers.title: Genome-resolved metagenomics reveals population-dependent gut microbiome responses to albendazole-ivermectin treatment
papers.abstract: Soil-transmitted helminth control relies on mass anthelmintic treatment, yet helminth-anthelmintic-microbiome interactions and their role on treatment response remain poorly understood. We characterised the microbiome, resistome, and functional profiles of 858 paired stool metagenomes from 429 children treated with albendazole or a fixed-dose albendazole-ivermectin co-formulation in the ALIVE clinical trial in Ethiopia and Mozambique. Baseline microbiome composition differed more by country than infection status and was not associated with albendazole efficacy or adverse events. Co-formulation treatment, particularly three consecutive daily doses, was associated with depletion of Enterobacteriaceae, predominantly Escherichia coli, in Ethiopia, with reductions in E. coli-associated resistance genes and metabolic pathways. Genome-resolved analyses of over 22,000 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes confirmed this depletion across multiple E. coli strain-level populations, linking taxonomic, resistome, and functional signals to one ecological event. These findings reveal an off-target effect of combination anthelmintic treatment relevant to large-scale deworming programmes and expand genomic resources for African gut microbiota.

papers.title: HLA-Resolve: Four-field HLA typing and MHC variant detection from long-read hybrid capture
papers.abstract: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is among the most polymorphic and difficult-to-genotype regions of the human genome. Accurate typing of its HLA genes, which encode antigen-presenting molecules, is critical for transplantation, pharmacogenomics, and disease-risk prediction. Long-read sequencing is increasingly used in HLA typing because of its ability to phase variants across long distances, but many long-read HLA typing workflows still rely on long-range PCR. Here, we present an end-to-end workflow for MHC genotyping that pairs hybrid capture with long-read sequencing on PacBio or Oxford Nanopore, using single-step enzymatic fragmentation and barcoding to enable automated library preparation. The hybrid capture panel enriches both classical and non-classical HLA Class I and Class II genes, as well as all 69 protein-coding MHC Class III genes. We introduce HLA-Resolve, a bioinformatic tool that types HLA genes from PacBio reads via phased full-gene sequence reconstruction, and we benchmark the capture assay and HLA-Resolve together across 32 geographically diverse samples. With PacBio data, variant calling achieved F1 scores of 99.8% for SNVs and 98.4% for indels against the Genome in a Bottle benchmark. HLA-Resolve showed 99.5% allele concordance with reference typings from the International Histocompatibility Working Group and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) at three-field resolution and 90.5% at four-field resolution, outperforming three other open-source long-read HLA typers on our HiFi hybrid capture reads. The full-gene sequences reconstructed by HLA-Resolve showed zero edit distance to the corresponding HPRC assemblies in 95% of comparisons. HLA-Resolve also showed high accuracy with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data, achieving 99.4% two-field concordance across 146 public PacBio WGS libraries and 99.5% three-field concordance across the 52 with full-resolution reference typings. Although developed for the MHC, the workflow is customizable to any gene set, providing a general framework for high-resolution genotyping.
